weaknesses: The headline comparison with Pic2Word is confounded. Table 1 explicitly states that its inversion network was trained with the original CLIP parameters, including when evaluated with fine-tuned encoders. This creates a representation mismatch that disadvantages the baseline. Table 2 partially addresses the issue, but a fully retrained, matched-backbone Pic2Word comparison and evaluation of the closely related textual-inversion method cited as [2] are needed to establish the claimed advantage.

Methodological originality is limited and insufficiently distinguished from prior work. Mapping image embeddings into pseudo-word tokens already underlies Pic2Word and related methods, while the encoder fine-tuning and matching losses reuse established techniques. Because dataset construction favors partially shared clothing, aggregate scores cannot establish how reliably the method preserves identity beyond residual appearance cues. The benchmark and alternative supervision are useful contributions, but the paper does not clearly establish a substantial technical advance beyond their combination.

Model selection is insufficiently separated from evaluation. ITCPR is designated exclusively for testing, yet Appendices C.3–C.5 select optimal architectures and fusion configurations using its results. No independent selection protocol or untouched final evaluation is described. Missing repeated runs or uncertainty estimates further limit conclusions about the smaller ablation and ensemble improvements.

ITCPR provides a potentially useful benchmark with 2,202 queries and a 20,510-image gallery drawn from three existing datasets.

The two-stage framework is coherent and relatively simple. Person-specific encoder fine-tuning followed by lightweight textual inversion enables composed retrieval without training on composed-query triplets. Retraining the closest baselines under matched encoders and training data is necessary to substantiate the headline superiority claim; this is the main reason for rejection.

Methodological originality is limited relative to the cited work. Image-to-pseudo-word mapping and composition through a frozen text encoder closely follow Pic2Word/SEARLE, while encoder fine-tuning uses established similarity-distribution and identity losses. ITCPR contributes 2,202 queries and a 20,510-image gallery, with manual annotation and an effort to identify missing positives.

Word4Per is a coherent, relatively simple framework that learns from existing person image–caption datasets without CPR training triplets. The lightweight inversion network and reported computational costs make the approach accessible.

strengths: The task is practically motivated: combining a reference photograph with an appearance update is a useful extension of composed image retrieval. ITCPR provides 2,202 queries against a 20,510-image gallery drawn from three real person-retrieval datasets.

The synthesis pipeline offers a practical way to address scarce training annotations. Combining bidirectional captions, jointly generated image pairs, and multimodal filtering produces a potentially valuable resource of 1.15 million training triplets.

The reported results support the usefulness of both the dataset and model. Training SPRC on SynCPR raises ITCPR Rank-1 from 25.07 to 42.27; FAFA further reaches 46.54. The separate CIRR experiment also favors FAFA over SPRC, 54.48 versus 51.96 Rank-1, providing evidence beyond the newly constructed benchmark.
The presentation is generally understandable, with helpful pipeline diagrams and substantial appendix material covering prompts, dataset construction, optimization settings, and ablations.
weaknesses: The main concern is evaluation independence. ITCPR is explicitly designated test-only, yet Sections 4.3 and C.4 select the soft-label strength, feature count, filtering threshold, auxiliary-loss weights, and masking ratio using reported ITCPR performance. No separate validation protocol or untouched final CPR evaluation is described. This apparent test-set tuning weakens confidence in the reported advantages.

The central claims of high-quality, identity-consistent synthetic data lack independent quantitative validation. There is no human audit reporting identity and caption error rates or calibration of the MLLM scores. Averaging four scores can also retain examples with weak identity consistency. Filtering and dataset-size experiments are useful, but matched-size downstream ablations of generator fine-tuning, joint versus independent generation, and LoRA-style mixing are missing.

The evidence that performance depends on complementary use of both modalities is incomplete. Although CaLa and SPRC are retrained on SynCPR, the image-only, text-only, and late-fusion baselines largely use different training datasets. Matched SynCPR-trained single-modality controls would distinguish compositional reasoning from domain adaptation and stronger representations.

ITCPR annotation reliability needs stronger support. Appendix B.1.2 describes checking the top-k neighbors returned by one visual encoder, without specifying k or estimating remaining missed positives. This procedure does not establish the claimed elimination of false negatives, particularly across appearance changes. Annotator agreement and a quantitative audit of relevance labels are also absent.

The masked reconstruction objective is underspecified. The decoder architecture and feature-normalization conventions are not provided. As written, the other losses depend on cosine similarity, so jointly rescaling embeddings and decoder outputs can reduce the reconstruction loss without improving alignment. The paper should explain what prevents this scale ambiguity.

FAFA's methodological novelty is incremental over BLIP-2 query features and established matching, diversity, and reconstruction objectives. The FDA comparison changes similarity aggregation and the matching objective together, leaving their contributions incompletely isolated. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported; adding MFR to FDA plus FD improves Rank-1 by only 0.49 percentage points and mAP by 0.11, making its contribution less convincing.

The privacy motivation and demographic-coverage claims are insufficiently substantiated. The generator is fine-tuned on real person photographs and the benchmark contains real identities, but the manuscript does not discuss relevant reuse conditions, memorization, demographic performance, or misuse through tracking people across clothing changes. Synthetic generation alone does not resolve these concerns.

strengths: CPR is a well-motivated, identity-preserving specialization of composed image retrieval. The million-scale SynCPR training set and manually annotated ITCPR benchmark address a meaningful data gap.

Generating paired images within one canvas is a practical synthesis idea. SynCPR substantially improves existing methods: SPRC’s ITCPR Rank-1 increases from 25.07% to 42.27%, providing evidence that the synthetic data transfers to real images.

weaknesses: The main concern is test-set-based model selection. Appendix B.1.3 designates ITCPR exclusively for testing, yet Section 4.3 and Appendix C.4 select alignment parameters, loss weights, masking ratio, and filtering threshold using its performance. No independent validation protocol is described. An identity-disjoint validation set and untouched final test evaluation are needed to substantiate the reported generalization gains.

The central data-quality claims exceed the evidence. Identity consistency, caption correctness, and demographic coverage are supported primarily by one MLLM’s scores and selected examples, without a random-sample human audit or measured residual error rates. Quantitative comparisons against independent image generation and generation without LoRA are also missing. ITCPR’s nearest-neighbor-assisted relabeling is useful, but its coverage and annotation reliability are not quantified.

The necessity of both query modalities is not convincingly isolated. Image-only, text-only, and late-fusion baselines use different training data and models. Matched-backbone baselines trained on SynCPR, together with reference-image removal or shuffling, would establish whether improvements reflect identity-sensitive composition rather than stronger training and target-attribute matching.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the appendix: the reconstruction decoder, feature dimensions, query-token count, KL stabilization constant, and minibatch policy for GID-related examples are unspecified. The latter directly affects whether group-label smoothing operates. No repeated runs or uncertainty estimates are provided, leaving smaller gains—such as the 0.11 mAP improvement from adding MFR to FDA+FD—uncertain.

The relationship to prior synthetic-triplet CIR work, including CompoDiff and CASE, needs clearer treatment. Dataset governance and privacy implications are under-discussed. Synthetic training examples do not resolve questions concerning reuse and redistribution of the real-person fine-tuning and benchmark images. The manuscript should document applicable permissions and discuss surveillance misuse and demographic limitations.

strengths: The paper makes a useful resource contribution by specializing composed retrieval to identity-constrained person search. SynCPR provides 1.15 million synthetic training triplets, while ITCPR provides 2,202 real-image queries against a 20,510-image gallery. Generating paired images within one canvas is a practical approach to encouraging identity consistency.

The experiments provide substantial evidence that SynCPR is useful beyond the proposed model: training on it increases CaLa’s Rank-1 from 24.02% to 39.33% and SPRC’s from 25.07% to 42.27%. FAFA further achieves 46.54% Rank-1 and 55.60% mAP, versus SPRC’s 42.27% and 51.62% with the same training dataset.

Component ablations support the proposed alignment approach: replacing ITC with FDA improves Rank-1 from 41.33% to 45.04%, with auxiliary objectives bringing it to 46.54%. The additional CIRR result, 54.48% versus SPRC’s 51.96% Rank-1, strengthens the evidence for usefulness beyond the authors’ benchmark.

The presentation is generally clear, with substantial appendix material covering prompts, generator adaptation, optimization, and annotation procedures. Manual verification of candidate false negatives is a valuable benchmark-construction step. Together, the resource value and consistent empirical gains support a borderline-accept recommendation.
weaknesses: The principal evaluation concern is model selection on the test benchmark. Section 4.3 and Appendix C.4 select the filtering threshold, alignment parameters, auxiliary-loss weights, and masking ratio using ITCPR performance, although Appendix B.1.3 describes its annotations as exclusively for testing. No separate validation protocol is reported, leaving the final CPR results vulnerable to selection bias.

Claims of high synthetic-data quality and comprehensive demographic coverage exceed the validation provided. Filtering relies on one MLLM without a reported independent human audit, identity-consistency error rate, or demographic analysis. Qualitative examples and downstream gains are encouraging, but controlled quantitative comparisons are also needed to establish the contributions of joint generation and LoRA adaptation.

The image-only, text-only, and late-fusion comparisons use different training data and architectures. Although the retrained CIR comparisons are valuable, matched modality ablations using SynCPR and the same backbone would better establish whether FAFA learns complementary identity and modification information.

FAFA’s architectural novelty is relatively incremental over established Q-Former, similarity aggregation, diversity regularization, and reconstruction ideas. Reproducibility also needs a precise decoder specification and ID/GID batch-construction procedure. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported, which particularly matters for the 0.49-point Rank-1 improvement from adding MFR to FDA plus FD.

Dataset documentation does not adequately address source-data usage permissions or privacy and surveillance implications. Synthetic training examples reduce additional collection requirements, but the generator adaptation and evaluation still use real-person images. These omissions warrant documentation rather than an assumption that synthetic generation resolves the relevant ethical concerns.
